Meanwhile the cavalry, all the noblest and chiefly those who were joined to Parmenion by near kinship, after report had spread abroad that Philotas was being tortured, fearing the law of the Macedonians, by which it was provided that the kinsmen of those who had plotted against the king should be put to death together with them, some killed themselves, others fled into pathless mountains and vast solitudes, a vast terror being spread through the whole camp, until the king, on learning of the disturbance, proclaimed that he remitted the law concerning the punishment of the kindred of the guilty.

11.21. Whether Philotas wished to free himself from torture by truth or by falsehood is a doubtful conjecture, since the same end of pain is set both for those who confess the truth and for those who tell lies.
11.22. But: "You are not ignorant," he said, "how familiarly my father lived with Hegelochus: that Hegelochus, I mean, who fell in battle: he was to us the cause of all our ills.

11.23. For when the king first ordered himself to be saluted as the son of Jupiter, he, taking it ill, said: 'Do we then acknowledge as king this man who disdains Philip as his father? It is all over with us, if we can endure such things.

11.24. He despises not only men but even the gods, who demands to be believed a god. We have lost Alexander, we have lost our king: we have fallen upon a pride tolerable neither to the gods, with whom he makes himself equal, nor to men, from whom he sets himself apart.
11.25. Have we made a god of our own blood, to despise us? to be burdened with coming into the assembly of mortals? Believe me, we too, if we are men, shall be adopted by the gods.
11.26. Who avenged the death of this man's great-grandfather Alexander, who then of Archelaus, who of Perdiccas, slain?

11.27. This man indeed pardoned his father's murderers.' These things Hegelochus said over supper: and on the next day at first light I am summoned by my father. He was sad, and saw me sorrowful: for we had heard things that bred anxiety.

11.28. So, that we might test whether he had poured out those words weighed down with wine, or had conceived them from a deeper design, it pleased us to summon him. He came, and, the same talk being repeated of his own accord, he added that, if we dared to be leaders, he would claim for himself the next part after us; if courage failed us, he would cover the design with silence.

11.29. To Parmenion, while Darius still lived, the thing seemed untimely: for they would be killing Alexander not for themselves but for the enemy; but with Darius removed, the reward of the king slain—Asia and the whole East—would fall to his murderers. And the design being approved, on these terms faith was both given and received.
11.30. As to what concerns Dymnus, I know nothing, and, having confessed these things, I understand that it does not avail me that I am free of the present crime."
11.31. They, the tortures being applied again, when with the very spear-shafts they beat his face and eyes, wrung from him that he should confess this charge too.

11.32. Then, as they demanded that he should set forth the order of the contemplated crime, since they seemed likely to detain the king long at Bactra, he answered that he had feared lest his father, seventy years old, the leader of so great an army, the keeper of so much money, should in the meantime be cut off, and there should be for himself, stripped of so great forces, no cause for killing the king.

11.33. That he had therefore hastened, while the reward was in his hands, to put the design into effect: and that, unless they believed his father absent from it, he did not, although he could no longer bear them, refuse the tortures.

11.34. They, having conferred, judging that enough had been inquired, returned to the king, who on the next day ordered both what Philotas had confessed to be read out, and the man himself, because he could not walk, to be carried in.

11.35. While he acknowledged everything, Demetrius, who was accused of being a partner in the most recent crime, was brought forward. With much affirmation and equal steadfastness of spirit and of face denying that anything had been contemplated by him against the king, he even demanded the tortures upon himself:

11.36. when Philotas, casting his eyes about, as they fell upon a certain Calas standing not far off, ordered him to come nearer. As the man, troubled, refused to pass over to him, he said: "Will you suffer Demetrius to lie and me to be tortured again?"

11.37. Calas's voice and blood had failed him, and the Macedonians suspected that Philotas wished to defile the innocent, because the young man had been named neither by Nicomachus nor by Philotas himself when he was tortured: but when he saw the king's officers standing around him, he confessed that he and Demetrius had contemplated that crime.
11.38. So all who had been named by Nicomachus were, the signal being given after the custom of their fathers, overwhelmed with stones.

11.39. From great peril not of his life only but also of ill will Alexander had been freed: for Parmenion and Philotas, the leading men of his friends, could not have been condemned, unless plainly guilty, without the indignation of the whole army.
11.40. And so, while the inquiry was doubtful, while he denied the crime, he seemed to be cruelly tortured: after his confession even the pity of his friends was idle.
